hints: Look carefully at the labelled cell surface membrane of the red blood cell in Fig. 1.1 and compare it with a normal smooth biconcave disc - what has happened to its shape?
Think about space - the central parent cell is surrounded by many small daughter cells with nuclei, so what will happen to the volume inside the red cell as they grow?
Remember the normal function of a red blood cell depends on haemoglobin - think about what the pathogen uses for growth and what that means for oxygen carriage and survival of the cell.
walkthrough:
See What The Diagram Shows**
A healthy red blood cell is a smooth biconcave disc with no nucleus. In Fig. 1.1 the labelled membrane is broken and irregular, and the inside is packed with many small cells each with a nucleus. That tells you the parasite is physically disrupting the host cell.

Link Growth To Bursting**
As the parent Plasmodium grows and produces many daughter cells, they fill the cytoplasm of the red cell. The membrane cannot stretch enough, so the cell bursts. This is haemolysis and the red cell dies.

Link Feeding To Loss Of Function**
Plasmodium feeds on haemoglobin for amino acids. Less haemoglobin means less oxygen can be taken up and transported. Toxins released when the cell bursts also cause disease symptoms.

Final answer: Cell loses biconcave shape / cell surface membrane becomes irregular; daughter cells fill the cell causing it to burst / haemolysis; haemoglobin is lost / used up so less / no oxygen is transported.

hints: Start with what must happen before any nucleus can divide - think about copying of genetic material so each daughter gets a full set.
Look at the number of nuclei in Fig. 1.1 - one parent has produced many daughters, so think about what type of nuclear division can be repeated to make many identical nuclei.
Think about how the cytoplasm is then shared out unequally around each nucleus to pinch off small separate cells.
walkthrough:
Copy The DNA First**
Before division the cell grows, synthesises proteins and new organelles, and replicates its DNA semi-conservatively. Each chromosome is copied so identical sister chromatids are available for each daughter.

Make Many Nuclei By Mitosis**
The nucleus then undergoes repeated mitosis - prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase - to produce many genetically identical nuclei. This is why you see a separate dark nucleus in each small daughter cell in Fig. 1.1.

Divide Cytoplasm Unequally**
Finally cytokinesis occurs unequally. Small amounts of cytoplasm are partitioned around each nucleus and daughter cells bud off from the parent, giving small identical cells ready to infect new red blood cells.
Final answer: DNA replication / synthesis; repeated mitosis to produce many / several nuclei; cytokinesis / budding off of daughter cells with unequal share of cytoplasm, all genetically identical.

hints: Recall the shape of the variable region of an antibody - how does it interact with an antigen on the surface of the pathogen?
Think about the journey of the pathogen in blood between liver cells and red blood cells - what would happen if its surface is covered?
Think about how phagocytes recognise antibody-coated pathogens - what part of the antibody helps them destroy it faster?
walkthrough:
Specific Binding**
Each antibody has a variable region complementary in shape to a specific antigen on the malarial pathogen. They combine to form an antibody-antigen complex. This is highly specific, like a lock and key.

Blocking Spread**
When free pathogens released from a burst red cell are coated with antibody, they cannot bind to and enter new red blood cells or liver cells. That directly interrupts spread through the bloodstream.

Marking For Destruction**
The constant region of the antibody is recognised by receptors on phagocytes. This is opsonisation. It stimulates phagocytosis, and clumping together of pathogens (agglutination) makes them easier to ingest and lyse.

Final answer: Antibodies complementary in shape bind to antigens / epitopes on pathogen; this prevents pathogen entering red blood cells / liver cells; antibodies act as opsonins marking pathogen for destruction by phagocytes / causing agglutination and lysis.

hints: Think beyond one person - what proportion of a population needs to be immune to slow transmission to those who are not vaccinated?
Think about people - why might some refuse a vaccine and what could health authorities do to encourage uptake, especially in children?
Think about the vaccine itself - what features of protection, such as how long it lasts and whether boosters are needed, make a programme easier?
Think about the pathogen - how would mutation to new strains make a vaccine less useful over time?
Think about practical logistics in hot countries - supply, storage temperature, shelf life, trained staff and cost of production and delivery.
walkthrough:
Protect Enough People**
Success depends on reaching the whole at-risk population, including children early in life before they are most at risk. When enough people are immune, herd immunity reduces transmission and protects even unvaccinated individuals.

Win Public Trust**
Education about benefits and safety is vital, plus active countering of anti-vaccination misinformation. Incentives, contact tracing to find at-risk people, and government funding all increase uptake.

Have A Practical Vaccine And Pathogen**
A good programme is helped by long duration of artificial immunity with no boosters, little mutation or antigenic change in the pathogen so the vaccine stays effective, and ability to update the vaccine if strains change.

Deliver It Reliably**
You need plentiful supply, long shelf life, stability at high temperatures or freeze-drying, simple administration by sufficient trained staff, and low production, storage, transport and delivery cost, ideally free to the patient.

Final answer: Any five: reach whole at-risk population to achieve herd immunity; vaccinate children early before peak risk; educate about benefits and counter misinformation; long-lasting protection with no boosters needed; little mutation / few strains so vaccine remains effective; plentiful supply, long shelf life and heat-stable; sufficient trained staff and low / funded cost.
